references.text: Jesus' parallel words in Matthew: 'Blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear. For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see but did not see it.' This is the closest parallel to Luke 10:23-24.
Isaiah prophesies about a people who see but do not understand – a contrast to the disciples' blessed eyes that truly see and understand what they witness in Jesus' ministry.
In Eden's garden, eyes were opened to see – but to sin and shame. In contrast, Jesus blesses the disciples' eyes that see God's work of salvation.
Simeon says that his eyes have seen God's salvation. Thematic parallel: seeing the fulfillment of God's promises with one's own eyes is a blessing.
Peter writes that the prophets searched and investigated the salvation that the disciples now have seen and experienced – they longed to see what the disciples saw, as Jesus says here.

The heroes of faith in the Old Testament saw the promises from afar and welcomed them, but did not experience their fulfillment. The disciples, however, got to see the fulfillment with their own eyes.
Jesus says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day; he saw it and was glad. This is linked to the theme that patriarchs and prophets longed to see the coming of the Messiah.
The immediate context: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit because the Father has revealed these things to the childlike. The disciples' blessed eyes are a result of this divine revelation.
Isaiah's prophecy about those who see that the Lord returns to Zion – 'they see with their own eyes.' The disciples are witnesses to God's work of salvation in Jesus.
'The ear that hears and the eye that sees – the Lord has made them both.' The disciples' ability to see and understand is a gift from God, which underscores the blessing in Luke 10:23.
